title.narrative: Stage 2 & 3 Blue Sky Localisation Initiative (DEC) - SLDP

description.narrative: Following the workshops conducted by the Syrian Civil Society Network Platform (SCNP) as part of Stage One of the DEC collective initiative (CI) “Blue Sky”, and the subsequent report produced, 3 themes were identified as key to accelerating localisation. We include here only some of the associated relevant summaries followed by a list of the actionable recommendations. To see the full list of findings and recommendations please refer to the Stage 1 final report, and the Blue-Sky workshop report. Following consultations with the collective initiative members, the Human Rights Due Diligence (HRDD) Project Design Tool was presented to the DEC as the recommended initiative to pilot. The rationale is that given localisation is taking time to implement throughout the sector (and is in fact stalling), project design could benefit from a “harm prevention” approach. The vision for the project is that the “HRDD” tool will support the mainstreaming of a human rights lens during programme design, both to prevent risk in complex emergencies, as well as raise awareness of human rights frameworks, resulting in staff being more aware of the potential, and future risks, associated with human rights in complex emergencies. Looking specifically to some of the Human rights violation in the context of northwest Syria, given to the understanding of Housing Land and Property (HLP) Rights within many organisations in NWS, it was obvious to them that the earthquake revealed that response activities could contribute to or exacerbate human rights violations. One well described issue was the rubble removal and rehabilitation of affected buildings without consideration for the complexity around HLP rights in NWS. Another example is low quality IDP housing projects. The most sustainable damage that low quality IDP housing projects could inflict on local communities is potentially on the environment. The larger the population in a given area, the greater the need for water to meet drinking and sanitation needs. In addition, construction projects require a lot of water, and all of this leads to great pressure on water resources in areas that already suffer from water shortages. Some donors are covering IDP housing projects without sufficient funding to establish proper cesspits which threatens water reserves and pollutes the soil because they are not equipped with layers of stones and sand to filter wastewater. A humanitarian responders lacked tools beyond monitoring and complaint systems to address these challenges.
